claim: A common CNS architecture is observed in all chordates, from vertebrates to basal chordates like the ascidian Ciona.
source: A common CNS architecture is observed in all chordates, from vertebrates to basal chordates like the ascidian Ciona.
evidence: This is a general statement about chordate CNS architecture that draws from established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Ciona stands apart among chordates in having a complete larval connectome.
source: Ciona stands apart among chordates in having a complete larval connectome.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Ryan et al., 2016 elsewhere in the manuscript describing the connectome completion.

claim: The first visuomotor circuit is characterized by glutamatergic photoreceptors and responds to the direction of light.
source: The first circuit is characterized by glutamatergic photoreceptors and responds to the direction of light.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in situ hybridization showing VGLUT expression and behavioral assays showing directional light response.

claim: Glutamatergic photoreceptors project to cholinergic motor neurons via two tiers of cholinergic interneurons.
source: These photoreceptors project to cholinergic motor neurons, via two tiers of cholinergic interneurons.
evidence: This is supported by connectome data and neurotransmitter expression mapping shown in the figures.

claim: The second visuomotor circuit responds to changes in ambient light and mediates an escape response.
source: The second circuit responds to changes in ambient light and mediates an escape response.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral assays showing dimming response described in the manuscript.

claim: The second circuit uses GABAergic photoreceptors which project to GABAergic interneurons, and then to cholinergic interneurons.
source: This circuit uses GABAergic photoreceptors which project to GABAergic interneurons, and then to cholinergic interneurons.
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data showing VGAT expression patterns and connectome connectivity data.

claim: The second circuit is disinhibitory.
source: Our observations on the behavior of larvae either treated with a GABA receptor antagonist or carrying a mutation that eliminates photoreceptors indicate the second circuit is disinhibitory.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data from picrotoxin treatment and frm mutant analysis.

claim: Ascidian larvae spend their first few days as free-swimming tadpole larvae.
source: At the start of their life, most ascidians spend their first few days as free-swimming tadpole larvae.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ascidian life cycle.

claim: Ascidian larvae display unmistakable chordate traits, including a prominent notochord running the length of a muscular tail and a dorsal central nervous system.
source: It is at the larval stage that ascidians display unmistakable chordate traits, including a prominent notochord running the length of a muscular tail and a dorsal central nervous system (CNS).
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge about ascidian larvae supported by citation to Satoh, 1994.

claim: Ascidian larvae attach via their adhesive palps and undergo metamorphosis into a sessile filter-feeding juvenile.
source: Ascidian morphology abruptly changes when the larvae attach via their adhesive palps and undergo metamorphosis, the product of which is a sessile filter-feeding juvenile with little resemblance to the larva (Satoh, 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Satoh, 1994.

claim: The Ciona larva measures only about 1 mm in length.
source: Ascidian larvae are small in comparison to vertebrate larvae, with the Ciona larva measuring only about 1 mm in length, with a total of ~2,600 cells (Satoh, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Satoh, 2014.

claim: The Ciona larva has a total of approximately 2,600 cells.
source: Ascidian larvae are small in comparison to vertebrate larvae, with the Ciona larva measuring only about 1 mm in length, with a total of ~2,600 cells (Satoh, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Satoh, 2014.

claim: The larval Ciona CNS has approximately 170 neurons.
source: Accordingly, the larval Ciona CNS is equally simple, having ~170 neurons (Ryan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ryan et al., 2016.

claim: Ciona larvae display negative gravitaxis and phototaxis.
source: Despite this simplicity, Ciona larvae display a range of integrated behaviors, including negative gravitaxis and phototaxis, and a response to dimming ambient light, all mediated by central sensory neurons.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Ciona larval behavior.

claim: Ciona larvae display a response to dimming ambient light mediated by central sensory neurons.
source: Despite this simplicity, Ciona larvae display a range of integrated behaviors, including negative gravitaxis and phototaxis, and a response to dimming ambient light, all mediated by central sensory neurons.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Ciona larval behavior.

claim: Ciona larvae have a mechanosensory/touch response mediated by peripheral sensory neurons.
source: Also well documented is a mechanosensory/touch response, and possibly chemosensation, mediated by peripheral sensory neurons (Ryan et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ryan et al., 2018.

claim: The Ciona larval brain vesicle is homologous to the vertebrate forebrain and midbrain.
source: Anatomically, the Ciona larval CNS is comprised anteriorly of the brain vesicle (BV; also known as the sensory vesicle), a region homologous to the vertebrate forebrain and midbrain, followed by the neck region, a homolog of the vertebrate midbrain/hindbrain junction (Figure 1).
evidence: This is an established anatomical homology in the field.

claim: The Ciona neck region is a homolog of the vertebrate midbrain/hindbrain junction.
source: Anatomically, the Ciona larval CNS is comprised anteriorly of the brain vesicle (BV; also known as the sensory vesicle), a region homologous to the vertebrate forebrain and midbrain, followed by the neck region, a homolog of the vertebrate midbrain/hindbrain junction (Figure 1).
evidence: This is an established anatomical homology in the field.

claim: The Ciona motor ganglion is thought to be homologous to the vertebrate hindbrain and/or spinal cord.
source: The MG is thought to be homologous to the vertebrate hindbrain and/or spinal cord, and contains ten motor neurons (MN) as well as a number of interneurons – including the two descending decussating neurons (ddN) which have been equated with vertebrate Mauthner cells which mediate the startle response (Ryan et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ryan et al., 2017.

claim: The Ciona motor ganglion contains ten motor neurons.
source: The MG is thought to be homologous to the vertebrate hindbrain and/or spinal cord, and contains ten motor neurons (MN) as well as a number of interneurons – including the two descending decussating neurons (ddN) which have been equated with vertebrate Mauthner cells which mediate the startle response (Ryan et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ryan et al., 2017.

claim: The two descending decussating neurons (ddN) have been equated with vertebrate Mauthner cells which mediate the startle response.
source: The MG is thought to be homologous to the vertebrate hindbrain and/or spinal cord, and contains ten motor neurons (MN) as well as a number of interneurons – including the two descending decussating neurons (ddN) which have been equated with vertebrate Mauthner cells which mediate the startle response (Ryan et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ryan et al., 2017.

claim: The Ciona larval nervous system has 6618 chemical synapses.
source: With the completion of a synaptic connectome from one larva, the Ciona larval nervous system is now one of the best described, with the connectome providing a detailed and quantitative connectivity matrix of the 6618 chemical and 1206 electrical CNS synapses (Ryan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ryan et al., 2016.

claim: The Ciona larval nervous system has 1206 electrical CNS synapses.
source: With the completion of a synaptic connectome from one larva, the Ciona larval nervous system is now one of the best described, with the connectome providing a detailed and quantitative connectivity matrix of the 6618 chemical and 1206 electrical CNS synapses (Ryan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ryan et al., 2016.

claim: The Ciona visual system is the best characterized of the larval sensory systems.
source: The Ciona visual system is the best characterized of the larval sensory systems (Kusakabe and Tsuda, 2007; Oonuma et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kusakabe and Tsuda, 2007 and Oonuma et al., 2016.

claim: The larval photoreceptors of Ciona are ciliary, like those of vertebrates.
source: The larval photoreceptors are ciliary, like those of vertebrates, and the photoreceptor opsins and visual cycle systems are, likewise, similar to those found in the vertebrate retina (Kusakabe and Tsuda, 2007; Kusakabe et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kusakabe and Tsuda, 2007 and Kusakabe et al., 2001.

claim: The photoreceptor opsins and visual cycle systems of Ciona are similar to those found in the vertebrate retina.
source: The larval photoreceptors are ciliary, like those of vertebrates, and the photoreceptor opsins and visual cycle systems are, likewise, similar to those found in the vertebrate retina (Kusakabe and Tsuda, 2007; Kusakabe et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kusakabe and Tsuda, 2007 and Kusakabe et al., 2001.

claim: The primary photoreceptive organ of Ciona is the ocellus, which consists of two groups of photoreceptors, three lens cells, and one pigment cell.
source: The primary photoreceptive organ of Ciona is the ocellus, which consists of two groups of photoreceptors, three lens cells, and one pigment cell.
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge about the Ciona ocellus.

claim: The first group of photoreceptors (PR-I) is comprised of 23 cells and clustered around the ocellus pigment cell.
source: The first group of photoreceptors (called here, PR-I) is comprised of 23 cells and clustered around the ocellus pigment cell (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by anatomical data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The opsin-containing outer segments of the PR-Is project into the cup shaped pigment cell.
source: The opsin-containing outer segments of the PR-Is project into the cup shaped pigment cell, making this group sensitive to the direction of incident light and thereby mediating negative phototaxis (Horie et al., 2008a; Salas et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Horie et al., 2008a and Salas et al., 2018.

claim: PR-I photoreceptors are sensitive to the direction of incident light and mediate negative phototaxis.
source: The opsin-containing outer segments of the PR-Is project into the cup shaped pigment cell, making this group sensitive to the direction of incident light and thereby mediating negative phototaxis (Horie et al., 2008a; Salas et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Horie et al., 2008a and Salas et al., 2018.

claim: The second group of ocellus photoreceptors (PR-II) is comprised of seven cells and is adjacent and anterior to the PR-Is.
source: The second group of ocellus photoreceptors (PR-II, Figure 1) is comprised of seven cells and is adjacent and anterior to the PR-Is, and is not associated with the pigment cell.
evidence: This is supported by anatomical data shown in Figure 1.

claim: PR-II photoreceptors are not associated with the pigment cell.
source: The second group of ocellus photoreceptors (PR-II, Figure 1) is comprised of seven cells and is adjacent and anterior to the PR-Is, and is not associated with the pigment cell.
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge.

claim: The PR-II cluster mediates the light dimming response, likely with a contribution from the PR-Is, by evoking highly tortuous and leftward-biased swims.
source: The PR-II cluster mediates the light dimming response, likely with a contribution from the PR-Is, by evoking highly tortuous and leftward-biased swims (Salas et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Salas et al., 2018.

claim: There is a third set of six photoreceptors (PR-IIIs) distal to the ocellus of unknown function.
source: There is a third set of six photoreceptors (PR-IIIs) distal to the ocellus of unknown function, although they are not involved in phototaxis or the dimming response (Horie et al., 2008a), nor do they make extensive connections to interneurons, as do the PR-I and -IIs (Ryan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Horie et al., 2008a and Ryan et al., 2016.

claim: PR-III photoreceptors are not involved in phototaxis or the dimming response.
source: There is a third set of six photoreceptors (PR-IIIs) distal to the ocellus of unknown function, although they are not involved in phototaxis or the dimming response (Horie et al., 2008a), nor do they make extensive connections to interneurons, as do the PR-I and -IIs (Ryan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Horie et al., 2008a and Ryan et al., 2016.

claim: PR-III photoreceptors do not make extensive connections to interneurons.
source: There is a third set of six photoreceptors (PR-IIIs) distal to the ocellus of unknown function, although they are not involved in phototaxis or the dimming response (Horie et al., 2008a), nor do they make extensive connections to interneurons, as do the PR-I and -IIs (Ryan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ryan et al., 2016.

claim: Vertebrates are characterized by the presence of paired lateral (retinal) eyes and an unpaired medial/pineal eye.
source: Vertebrates are characterized by the presence of paired lateral (i.e., retinal) eyes, as well as an unpaired medial/pineal eye (Lamb et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lamb et al., 2007.

claim: The cephalochordate Amphioxus has four distinct photoreceptive organs.
source: The cephalochordate Amphioxus by contrast, has four distinct photoreceptive organs (Pergner and Kozmik, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pergner and Kozmik, 2017.

claim: The amphioxus frontal eye has been proposed as homologous to the vertebrate lateral eyes.
source: The amphioxus frontal eye has been proposed as homologous to the vertebrate lateral eyes, while the lamellar body is thought to be homologous to the vertebrate pineal organ (Pergner and Kozmik, 2017; Vopalensky et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Pergner and Kozmik, 2017 and Vopalensky et al., 2012.

claim: The amphioxus lamellar body is thought to be homologous to the vertebrate pineal organ.
source: The amphioxus frontal eye has been proposed as homologous to the vertebrate lateral eyes, while the lamellar body is thought to be homologous to the vertebrate pineal organ (Pergner and Kozmik, 2017; Vopalensky et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Pergner and Kozmik, 2017 and Vopalensky et al., 2012.

claim: The amphioxus dorsal ocelli and Joseph cells are thought to be vestiges of a more primitive photoreceptive system based on their rhabdomeric morphology.
source: The other two amphioxus photoreceptor types, the dorsal ocelli and the Joseph cells, are thought, based on a number of criteria, including their rhabdomeric morphology- which differs from the ciliary morphology of vertebrate and ascidian photoreceptors- to be vestiges of a more primitive photoreceptive system.
evidence: This is an inference based on morphological comparisons.

claim: The ascidian ocellus has been proposed as having homology to either the medial or the retinal eyes.
source: Based on various criteria the ascidian ocellus has been proposed as having homology to either the medial or the retinal eyes (Kusakabe et al., 2001; Lamb et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kusakabe et al., 2001 and Lamb et al., 2007.

claim: The Ciona connectome predicts the neural circuitry linking photoreceptors to motor activation.
source: The Ciona larval connectome predicts the neural circuity linking photoreceptors to motor activation (Ryan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ryan et al., 2016.

claim: The six photoreceptor RNs (prRN) receive input exclusively from the PR-I photoreceptors.
source: The six photoreceptor RNs (prRN) receive input exclusively from the PR-I photoreceptors and then project posteriorly to the paired right/left MG interneurons (three on each side; MGIN in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by connectome data shown in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The prRNs project posteriorly to the paired right/left MG interneurons.
source: The six photoreceptor RNs (prRN) receive input exclusively from the PR-I photoreceptors and then project posteriorly to the paired right/left MG interneurons (three on each side; MGIN in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by connectome data shown in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: There are eight photoreceptor ascending MG RNs (pr-AMG RN) that are postsynaptic to both the PR-I and PR-II photoreceptors.
source: A second cluster of eight RNs, the photoreceptor ascending MG RNs (pr-AMG RN) are postsynaptic to both the PR-I and PR-II photoreceptors, and are so-named because they, unlike the prRNs, receive input from the ascending MG peripheral interneurons (AMG neurons; not shown in Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by connectome data.

claim: The pr-AMG RNs receive input from the ascending MG peripheral interneurons (AMG neurons).
source: A second cluster of eight RNs, the photoreceptor ascending MG RNs (pr-AMG RN) are postsynaptic to both the PR-I and PR-II photoreceptors, and are so-named because they, unlike the prRNs, receive input from the ascending MG peripheral interneurons (AMG neurons; not shown in Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by connectome data.

claim: There are extensive synaptic connections between the pr-AMG RNs and the prRNs.
source: There are also extensive synaptic connections between the pr-AMG RNs and the prRNs.
evidence: This is supported by connectome data.

claim: The pr-AMG RNs project posteriorly to the left and right MGINs.
source: Like the prRNs, the pr-AMG RNs project posteriorly to the left and right MGINs.
evidence: This is supported by connectome data.

claim: The MGINs synapse onto the paired right and left motor neurons.
source: The MGINs in turn synapse onto the paired right and left motor neurons (five on each side).
evidence: This is supported by connectome data.

claim: The Ciona PR-I circuit is an excitatory relay from glutamatergic photoreceptors signaling to AMPA receptors on cholinergic prRNs.
source: We find that the PR-I circuit is an excitatory relay from glutamatergic photoreceptors signaling to AMPA receptors on cholinergic prRNs.
evidence: This is supported by neurotransmitter expression data and pharmacological experiments with perampanel.

claim: The PR-II circuit initiates with GABAergic photoreceptors synapsing onto GABAergic pr-AMG RNs.
source: On the other hand, the PR-II circuit initiates with GABAergic photoreceptors synapsing onto GABAergic pr-AMG RNs.
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data showing VGAT expression.

claim: The sequential array of GABAergic neurons in the PR-II pathway supports a model in which this circuit is disinhibitory.
source: Both the sequential array of GABAergic neurons in this pathway and the behavior of larvae treated with GABA inhibitors, or carrying a mutation that misspecifies the anterior BV, support a model in which this circuit is disinhibitory.
evidence: This is supported by neurotransmitter expression data and behavioral experiments.

claim: The behavior of larvae treated with GABA inhibitors supports a disinhibitory model for the PR-II circuit.
source: Both the sequential array of GABAergic neurons in this pathway and the behavior of larvae treated with GABA inhibitors, or carrying a mutation that misspecifies the anterior BV, support a model in which this circuit is disinhibitory.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral experiments with picrotoxin.

claim: The behavior of larvae carrying a mutation that misspecifies the anterior BV supports a disinhibitory model for the PR-II circuit.
source: Both the sequential array of GABAergic neurons in this pathway and the behavior of larvae treated with GABA inhibitors, or carrying a mutation that misspecifies the anterior BV, support a model in which this circuit is disinhibitory.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral experiments with frm mutants.

claim: The ocellus is reported to have widespread VGLUT expression, indicating that the Ciona photoreceptors are glutamatergic.
source: For example, the ocellus is reported to have widespread VGLUT expression, indicating that the Ciona photoreceptors, like those of vertebrates are glutamatergic (Horie et al., 2008b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Horie et al., 2008b.

claim: The expression domains of both VGAT and glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD) are suggestive of a subpopulation of GABAergic/glycinergic photoreceptors.
source: However, the expression domains of both VGAT and glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD) are suggestive of a subpopulation of GABAergic/glycinergic photoreceptors (Yoshida et al., 2004; Zega et al., 2008), although the identities of these cells within the ocellus is not known.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Yoshida et al., 2004 and Zega et al., 2008.

claim: A subset of photoreceptors coexpress pVGAT>kaede and pOpsin1>RFP at the anterior and ventral sides of the ocellus.
source: To investigate this further, fertilized eggs from a stable transgenic Ciona line expressing kaede fluorescent protein under the VGAT promoter (pVGAT > kaede) (Horie et al., 2011) were microinjected with a pOpsin1 > red fluorescent protein (RFP) construct (Kusakabe et al., 2001; Kusakabe et al., 2004) (Figure 2a; n = 5 larvae observed). We observed a subset of photoreceptors coexpressing the two fluorescent markers both at the anterior and ventral sides of the ocellus (white and orange arrowheads, respectively).
evidence: This is supported by transgenic reporter expression data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: VGLUT is expressed in the ocellus, the two otolith antenna cells, and in epidermal sensory neurons.
source: In agreement with previous reports (Horie et al., 2008b) we observed VGLUT expression in the ocellus (blue arrowhead), the two otolith antenna cells (AC), and in epidermal sensory neurons (red arrowheads).
evidence: This is supported by HCR in situ data shown in Figure 2b and citation to Horie et al., 2008b.

claim: VGAT is expressed in two separate clusters within the ocellus.
source: Consistent with the above transgenic data, VGAT was expressed in two separate clusters within the ocellus (white and orange arrowheads), as well as in a separate group of BV neurons outside the ocellus corresponding to previously described VGAT-positive neurons that project axons to the MG (Yoshida et al., 2004) (labeled in Figure 2b as RNs, see next section).
evidence: This is supported by HCR in situ data shown in Figure 2b and citation to Yoshida et al., 2004.

claim: The anterior VGAT-expressing photoreceptor cluster consisted of 7 cells (±1 cell, n = 17 larvae).
source: The anterior VGAT-expressing photoreceptor cluster consisted of 7 cells (±1 cell, n = 17 larvae), while the posterior group consisted of two cells (n = 20 larvae).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of HCR in situ data.

claim: The posterior VGAT-expressing photoreceptor cluster consisted of two cells (n = 20 larvae).
source: The anterior VGAT-expressing photoreceptor cluster consisted of 7 cells (±1 cell, n = 17 larvae), while the posterior group consisted of two cells (n = 20 larvae).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of HCR in situ data.

claim: A subset of VGAT-expressing cells in both the anterior and posterior photoreceptor clusters also expressed VGLUT.
source: We also observed a subset of the VGAT-expressing cells in both the anterior and posterior clusters that also expressed VGLUT (Figure 2c and d).
evidence: This is supported by double HCR in situ data shown in Figure 2c and d.

claim: In the anterior photoreceptor cluster, 2 cells (±1; n = 4) at the anterior edge exclusively expressed VGAT.
source: In the anterior cluster, we observed that the 2 cells (±1; n = 4 VGAT/VGLUT double in situ larvae) at the anterior edge exclusively expressed VGAT (white arrowheads in Figure 2c), while the four cells immediately posterior to these cells co-expressed VGAT and VGLUT.
evidence: This is supported by double HCR in situ data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Four cells in the anterior photoreceptor cluster co-expressed VGAT and VGLUT.
source: In the anterior cluster, we observed that the 2 cells (±1; n = 4 VGAT/VGLUT double in situ larvae) at the anterior edge exclusively expressed VGAT (white arrowheads in Figure 2c), while the four cells immediately posterior to these cells co-expressed VGAT and VGLUT.
evidence: This is supported by double HCR in situ data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: In the posterior photoreceptor cluster, one of two cells co-expressed VGAT and VGLUT, while the other only expressed VGAT (n = 5).
source: In the posterior cluster we observed in all samples (n = 5) that one of two cells co-expressed VGAT and VGLUT, while the other only expressed VGAT (Figure 2c, orange arrowheads).
evidence: This is supported by double HCR in situ data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: The PR-IIs are VGAT-positive, with a subset co-expressing VGLUT.
source: Given the cellular anatomy of the Ciona ocellus, with seven PR-IIs anterior and 23 PR-Is posterior (Ryan et al., 2016; Horie et al., 2008a), and our transgenic and HCR in situ results, we assign the PR-IIs as being VGAT-positive, with a subset co-expressing VGLUT (Figure 2d).
evidence: This is an inference based on anatomical position and expression data, supported by citations to Ryan et al., 2016 and Horie et al., 2008a.

claim: The anterior/ventral location of the two VGAT-only PR-IIs suggests that they are PR-b and PR-e.
source: The anterior/ventral location of the two VGAT-only PR-IIs suggest that they are PR-b and –e (Figure 2c and d).
evidence: This is an inference based on anatomical position shown in Figure 2c and d.

claim: The majority of the PR-Is are exclusively glutamatergic with the exception of two ventral cells.
source: By contrast, the majority of the PR-Is are exclusively glutamatergic with the exception of two ventral cells, one co-expressing VGAT and VGLUT and the other expressing only VGAT.
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data.

claim: Registration of cell centroids from multiple in situ datasets with the connectome ssEM dataset is meaningful if there is strong stereotypy in the number and position of neurons among Ciona larvae.
source: To get a better indication of the identities of these two cells we performed a registration of cell centroids from multiple in situ datasets (n = 11) with the centroids from the connectome serial section electron microscopy (ssEM) dataset. This registration would only be meaningful if there is strong stereotypy in the number and position of the neurons among Ciona larvae.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the requirements for valid registration.

claim: The ocellus photoreceptor somata and their outer segments are arranged in rows, suggesting an ordered cellular architecture.
source: The ocellus photoreceptor somata and their outer segments are known to be arranged in rows, suggesting an ordered cellular architecture (Ryan et al., 2016; Horie et al., 2008a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ryan et al., 2016 and Horie et al., 2008a.

claim: Convergence of NT type with registered photoreceptors would be taken as evidence of stereotypy and of the validity of making NT use predictions.
source: Convergence of NT type with registered photoreceptors (both between HCR in situ samples and between these and the ssEM sample) would be taken as evidence of stereotypy, and of the validity of making NT use predictions.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the interpretation of registration results.

claim: Among the PR-Is, PR-9 is likely to be exclusively VGAT-positive.
source: From the matrix we observed strong overall support for the registration, although with variable confidence for each photoreceptor. The heat map indicates that among the PR-Is, PR-9 is likely to be exclusively VGAT-positive, while PR-10 is likely to be both VGAT- and VGLUT-positive.
evidence: This is supported by registration analysis shown in Figure 2e.

claim: PR-10 is likely to be both VGAT- and VGLUT-positive.
source: From the matrix we observed strong overall support for the registration, although with variable confidence for each photoreceptor. The heat map indicates that among the PR-Is, PR-9 is likely to be exclusively VGAT-positive, while PR-10 is likely to be both VGAT- and VGLUT-positive.
evidence: This is supported by registration analysis shown in Figure 2e.

claim: The confusion matrix gives high confidence to the assignment of PR-9 and PR-10 neurotransmitter identities.
source: The confusion matrix gives high confidence to this assignment, particularly for PR-9.
evidence: This is supported by the confusion matrix shown in Figure 2f.

claim: The connectivity of PR-9 and PR-10 in the visuomotor pathway does not appear to be qualitatively different than the other PR-Is.
source: Although PR-9 and PR-10 appear to stand out from the other PR-Is in their NT use, the connectivity of these two photoreceptors in the visuomotor pathway does not appear to be qualitatively different than the other PR-Is (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by connectivity data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The heat map confirms that the other PR-Is are exclusively VGLUT, however with lower confidence for PR-16.
source: Finally, the heat map confirms that the other PR-Is are exclusively VGLUT, however with lower confidence for PR-16, which failed to register well.
evidence: This is supported by the heat map shown in Figure 2e.

claim: Sensory input from the photoreceptors, antenna cells, coronet cells, bipolar tail neurons and a subset of peripheral neurons is directed to a cluster of approximately 30 RNs in the pBV.
source: Sensory input from the photoreceptors, antenna cells, coronet cells, bipolar tail neurons and a subset of peripheral neurons is directed to a cluster of ~30 RNs in the pBV.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Ciona neural connectivity.

claim: The pBV RNs extend axons through the neck to the MG.
source: These RNs in turn extend axons through the neck to the MG.
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge.

claim: Previous in situ hybridization studies identified VGAT- and VACHT-expressing neurons in the appropriate place in the BV to be RNs.
source: Previous in situ hybridization studies identified VGAT- and VACHT-expressing neurons in the appropriate place in the BV to be RNs (Yoshida et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yoshida et al., 2004.

claim: VGAT- and VACHT-expressing neurons in the BV project axons posteriorly to the MG.
source: Moreover, these neurons project axons posteriorly to the MG, a defining characteristic of the pBV RNs.
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge.

claim: BV neurons expressing glutamate, dopamine, and serotonin are neither in the correct brain region to be RNs, nor do they project from the BV to the MG.
source: BV neurons expressing other major NTs, including glutamate, dopamine, and serotonin, are neither in the correct brain region to be RNs, nor do they project from the BV to the MG ([Horie et al., 2008b; Moret et al., 2005; Pennati et al., 2007], and our observations).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Horie et al., 2008b, Moret et al., 2005, and Pennati et al., 2007, as well as the authors' own observations.

claim: The pBV RNs cluster in two distinct groups along the anterior/posterior axis, with the anterior cluster expressing VACHT, and the posterior group expressing VGAT.
source: By HCR in situ we observed that the pBV RNs cluster in two distinct groups along the anterior/posterior axis, with the anterior cluster expressing VACHT, and the posterior group expressing VGAT (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is supported by HCR in situ data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: An average of 16 (±1.6, n = 9 larvae) VGAT-positive neurons were observed in the pBV RN cluster.
source: We observed an average of 16 (±1.6, n = 9 larvae) VGAT-positive neurons and 11 (±1, n = 8 larvae) VACHT-positive neurons.
evidence: This is supported by quantification of HCR in situ data.

claim: An average of 11 (±1, n = 8 larvae) VACHT-positive neurons were observed in the pBV RN cluster.
source: We observed an average of 16 (±1.6, n = 9 larvae) VGAT-positive neurons and 11 (±1, n = 8 larvae) VACHT-positive neurons.
evidence: This is supported by quantification of HCR in situ data.

claim: The confusion matrix for the RNs shows a lower level of convergence than for the PR-Is, suggesting that the cellular anatomy of the RN cluster is less structured than the ocellus.
source: The confusion matrix for the RNs shows a lower level of convergence than for the PR-Is, suggesting that the cellular anatomy of the RN cluster is less structured than the ocellus (Figure 3b; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an inference based on the confusion matrix shown in Figure 3b.

claim: The RNs are most often confused for other RNs of the same class.
source: However, the confusion matrix also shows that the RNs are most often confused for other RNs of the same class (white boxes in Figure 3b).
evidence: This is supported by the confusion matrix shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Higher confidence can be had in the NT use by RN class than in individual neuron identities.
source: This is most evident when the registration is performed not with single cells, but with pooled RNs of each class (Figure 3c), and is presumably a reflection of the clustering of RN classes in the pBV. Thus we can have higher confidence in the NT use by RN class than we can have in individual neuron identities.
evidence: This is an inference based on the confusion matrix shown in Figure 3c.

claim: The registration predicts that eight of the ten AntRNs are VGAT positive.
source: For example, the connectome shows the AntRNs are clustered at the rear of the BV (Figure 3—figure supplement 1; (Ryan et al., 2016)), as are the VGAT expressing neurons (Figure 3a; Figure 3—figure supplement 1). Accordingly, the registration predicts that eight of the ten AntRNs are VGAT positive (Figure 3c).
evidence: This is an inference based on registration analysis shown in Figure 3c and supported by citation to Ryan et al., 2016.

claim: The registration predicts that five of the eight pr-AMG RNs are VGAT expressing.
source: For the present study, which focuses on the visuomotor pathway, the registration predicts that five of the eight pr-AMG RNs are VGAT expressing, two are VACHT expressing, and one (pr-AMG RN 157) cannot be resolved (no dual VGAT/VACHT expression was observed in the in situs).
evidence: This is an inference based on registration analysis.

claim: The registration predicts that two of the eight pr-AMG RNs are VACHT expressing.
source: For the present study, which focuses on the visuomotor pathway, the registration predicts that five of the eight pr-AMG RNs are VGAT expressing, two are VACHT expressing, and one (pr-AMG RN 157) cannot be resolved (no dual VGAT/VACHT expression was observed in the in situs).
evidence: This is an inference based on registration analysis.

claim: One pr-AMG RN (pr-AMG RN 157) cannot be resolved for neurotransmitter identity.
source: For the present study, which focuses on the visuomotor pathway, the registration predicts that five of the eight pr-AMG RNs are VGAT expressing, two are VACHT expressing, and one (pr-AMG RN 157) cannot be resolved (no dual VGAT/VACHT expression was observed in the in situs).
evidence: This is an inference based on registration analysis.

claim: The registration predicts that the six prRNs are evenly mixed between VGAT and VACHT expression.
source: On the other hand, the registration predicts that the six prRNs are evenly mixed between VGAT and VACHT expression.
evidence: This is an inference based on registration analysis.

claim: The MG contains five left/right pairs of motor neurons.
source: The MG contains five left/right pairs of motor neurons, as well as several classes of interneurons, including six MGINs, seven AMGs, two ddNs, and two posterior MG interneurons (Ryan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ryan et al., 2016.

claim: The MG contains six MGINs, seven AMGs, two ddNs, and two posterior MG interneurons.
source: The MG contains five left/right pairs of motor neurons, as well as several classes of interneurons, including six MGINs, seven AMGs, two ddNs, and two posterior MG interneurons (Ryan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ryan et al., 2016.

claim: Two left/right pairs of decussating VGAT-positive neurons are described in the MG.
source: Also described in the MG are two left/right pairs of decussating VGAT-positive neurons (Horie et al., 2009; Nishino et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Horie et al., 2009 and Nishino et al., 2010.

claim: The decussating VGAT-positive neurons are likely the same as the decussating MG neurons described in the connectome.
source: These are likely the same decussating MG neurons as described in the connectome, although the names are slightly different (anterior caudal inhibitory neurons (Horie et al., 2009) versus ascending contralateral inhibitory neurons (Ryan et al., 2016), both abbreviated as ACIN).
evidence: This is an inference based on anatomical similarity, supported by citations to Horie et al., 2009 and Ryan et al., 2016.

claim: The connectome reports only three ACINs, with the anterior ACIN not paired.
source: However, the connectome reports only three ACINs, with the anterior ACIN not paired.
evidence: This is a statement about the connectome data.

claim: The unpaired anterior ACIN was speculated to be an anomalous feature of the particular larva used for the ssEM.
source: It was speculated that this was an anomalous feature of the particular larva used for the ssEM.
evidence: This is speculation about the connectome data.

claim: A second larva being analyzed by ssEM for connectomics shows two pairs of ACINs.
source: Supporting this, a second larva being analyzed by ssEM for connectomics shows two pairs of ACINs (K. Ryan, personal communication).
evidence: This is supported by personal communication with K. Ryan.

claim: The MG has a well-defined anterior-to-posterior and dorsal-to-ventral cellular anatomy.
source: Like the ocellus, the MG has a well-defined anterior-to-posterior and dorsal-to-ventral cellular anatomy (Figure 4a and b; Ryan et al., 2016; Ryan et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 4a and b and citations to Ryan et al., 2016 and Ryan et al., 2018.

claim: The motor neurons are cholinergic.
source: Neurotransmitter use by some MG neurons is already documented, including the motor neurons, which are cholinergic (Takamura et al., 2010; Takamura et al., 2002), and the ACINs which are glycinergic (Nishino et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Takamura et al., 2010 and Takamura et al., 2002.

claim: The ACINs are glycinergic.
source: Neurotransmitter use by some MG neurons is already documented, including the motor neurons, which are cholinergic (Takamura et al., 2010; Takamura et al., 2002), and the ACINs which are glycinergic (Nishino et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Nishino et al., 2010.

claim: VGAT- and VACHT-positive neurons were observed in the MG by HCR in situ hybridization.
source: By HCR in situ hybridization we observed VGAT- and VACHT-positive neurons in the MG (Figure 4b), but no VGLUT- or TH-positive cells (data not shown).
evidence: This is supported by HCR in situ data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: No VGLUT- or TH-positive cells were observed in the MG.
source: By HCR in situ hybridization we observed VGAT- and VACHT-positive neurons in the MG (Figure 4b), but no VGLUT- or TH-positive cells (data not shown).
evidence: This is supported by the authors' experimental observations.

claim: These results are consistent with previous studies showing no VGLUT or TH expression in the MG.
source: These results are consistent with previous studies (Horie et al., 2008b; Moret et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Horie et al., 2008b and Moret et al., 2005.

claim: No serotonergic cells were reported to be present in the MG.
source: Likewise it was reported that no serotonergic cells were present in the MG (Pennati et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pennati et al., 2007.

claim: The VGAT- and VACHT-expressing neurons in the MG are segregated anatomically.
source: As with the RNs, the VGAT- and VACHT-expressing neurons in the MG are segregated anatomically.
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data.

claim: A population of 6-7 cells between the AMGs and the MNs failed to label with any NT markers and are hypothesized to be ependymal cells.
source: We also found a population of 6–7 cells between the AMGs and the MNs (asterisks in Figure 4a), that were not annotated in the connectome as neurons and that failed to label with any of our NT markers. We hypothesize that these are ependymal cells, which are abundant in the nerve cord immediately caudal to this region.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the lack of NT marker expression and anatomical position shown in Figure 4a.

claim: The anterior group of VGAT-positive cells in the MG is clustered dorsally and corresponds to AMGs.
source: Because of the highly structured MG cellular anatomy, we can identify the various MG cell types in the in situ data. The anterior group of VGAT-positive cells is clustered dorsally in the MG, and correspond to AMGs (4 c, d and e; (Ryan et al., 2017)).
evidence: This is an inference based on anatomical position shown in Figure 4c, d, and e, supported by citation to Ryan et al., 2017.

claim: In a dorsal view of the MG, a ring of VGAT-positive cells was observed with a non-VGAT expressing cell in the center.
source: In a dorsal view of the MG (Figure 4f,g and h) a ring of VGAT-positive cells was observed with a non-VGAT expressing cell in the center (asterisk, Figure 4f and g).
evidence: This is supported by in situ data shown in Figure 4f and g.

claim: The VGAT-expressing cells in the AMG ring appear to be AMGs 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, and 7.
source: The VGAT-expressing cells appear to be AMGs 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, and 7, while the central cell, which is instead positive for VACHT, appears to be AMG5.
evidence: This is an inference based on anatomical position and expression patterns.

claim: The central non-VGAT expressing cell in the AMG ring is positive for VACHT and appears to be AMG5.
source: The VGAT-expressing cells appear to be AMGs 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, and 7, while the central cell, which is instead positive for VACHT, appears to be AMG5.
evidence: This is an inference based on anatomical position and expression patterns.

claim: The connectome shows that AMG5 differs in its connectivity from the other AMGs.
source: The connectome shows that AMG5 differs in its connectivity from the other AMGs.
evidence: This is a statement about connectome data.

claim: AMG5 is the principle synaptic input for PNS neurons.
source: Significantly, AMG5 is the principle synaptic input for PNS neurons.
evidence: This is a statement about connectome data.

claim: AMG5 synapses to the other AMGs, which in turn project their axons to other cells in the MG.
source: It then synapses to the other AMGs, which in turn project their axons to other cells in the MG, including MGINs and MNs, as well as to the pr-AMG RNs in the BV.
evidence: This is a statement about connectome data.

claim: Two pairs of VGAT-positive neurons were observed in the posterior of the MG.
source: In the posterior of the MG we observed two pairs of VGAT-positive neurons, as described previously (Horie et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by in situ data and citation to Horie et al., 2009.

claim: A continuous block of VACHT expression was observed in the ventral MG that encompasses the anterior three pairs of MNs, the ddNs, and the MGINs.
source: Finally, in the ventral MG we observed a continuous block of VACHT expression that encompasses the anterior three pairs of MNs, the ddNs, and the MGINs.
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data.

claim: Similar in situ patterns were observed in most larvae.
source: Similar in situ patterns were observed in most larvae (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), although the positions of the ACINs were offset in several (see larvae 5 and 6 in Figure 4—figure supplement 1), and one larva was observed to be missing both one motor neuron and one ACIN (larva 7in Figure 4—figure supplement 1), suggesting that MG variants, such as was observed in the animal used in the connectome study, may be relatively common.
evidence: This is supported by in situ data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: MG variants may be relatively common.
source: Similar in situ patterns were observed in most larvae (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), although the positions of the ACINs were offset in several (see larvae 5 and 6 in Figure 4—figure supplement 1), and one larva was observed to be missing both one motor neuron and one ACIN (larva 7in Figure 4—figure supplement 1), suggesting that MG variants, such as was observed in the animal used in the connectome study, may be relatively common.
evidence: This is speculation based on observed variability in in situ data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The PR-Is, with the exception of two cells, are glutamatergic.
source: Our results indicate that the PR-Is, with the exception of two cells, are glutamatergic, while the PR-IIs are a mixture of GABAergic and GABA/glutamatergic.
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data.

claim: The PR-IIs are a mixture of GABAergic and GABA/glutamatergic photoreceptors.
source: Our results indicate that the PR-Is, with the exception of two cells, are glutamatergic, while the PR-IIs are a mixture of GABAergic and GABA/glutamatergic.
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data.

claim: The Ciona genome contains a single glutamate AMPA receptor (AMPAR).
source: The Ciona genome contains a single glutamate AMPA receptor (AMPAR) (Okamura et al., 2005) that is expressed in larvae in the two antenna cells, and in a small cluster of neurons in the pBV (Hirai et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Okamura et al., 2005 and Hirai et al., 2017.

claim: The AMPAR is expressed in larvae in the two antenna cells and in a small cluster of neurons in the pBV.
source: The Ciona genome contains a single glutamate AMPA receptor (AMPAR) (Okamura et al., 2005) that is expressed in larvae in the two antenna cells, and in a small cluster of neurons in the pBV (Hirai et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hirai et al., 2017.

claim: Most of the pBV group of AMPAR-positive neurons are clustered at the ends of Arrestin-labeled photoreceptor axons.
source: Published results show that most of the pBV group of AMPAR-positive neurons are clustered at the ends of Arrestin-labeled photoreceptor axons, and that they extend their axons to the MG, suggesting they are photoreceptor RNs (see Figure 2B" in Hirai et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hirai et al., 2017.

claim: The pBV AMPAR-positive neurons extend their axons to the MG, suggesting they are photoreceptor RNs.
source: Published results show that most of the pBV group of AMPAR-positive neurons are clustered at the ends of Arrestin-labeled photoreceptor axons, and that they extend their axons to the MG, suggesting they are photoreceptor RNs (see Figure 2B" in Hirai et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an inference based on anatomical connectivity, supported by citation to Hirai et al., 2017.

claim: The pBV group of AMPAR-positive neurons is composed of approximately 6 cells.
source: We find that this pBV group is composed of ~6 cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Coexpression of the AMPAR reporter was observed in a subset of the VACHT-positive RNs, but never in the VGAT-expressing RNs.
source: To investigate this further, we co-expressed an pAMPAR >GFP construct (Hirai et al., 2017) with pVACHT >CFP and pVGAT >nuclear RFP constructs. We observed coexpression of the AMPAR reporter in a subset of the VACHT-positive RNs, but never in the VGAT-expressing RNs (Figure 5a).
evidence: This is supported by transgenic reporter coexpression data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: Perampanel-treated larvae do not show negative phototaxis.
source: Figure 5b and c show representative frames from the time-lapse capture at the start and at 60 min for control and perampanel-treated larvae, respectively. In the control sample the larvae at 60 min were observed to cluster at the side of the petri dish away from the light (distal side; red arrows in Figure 5b). By contrast no taxis was observed in the perampanel treated larvae (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral assay data shown in Figure 5b and c.

claim: For control larvae approximately 70% swam to the distal third within 1 hr during phototaxis assay.
source: Combined results from three independent assays (n = 129–365 larvae per group) are shown in Figure 5d and presented as the percent of larvae found on distal third of the petri dish. For control larvae ~ 70% swam to the distal third within 1 hr, while the perampanel-treated larvae remained evenly distributed across the dish.
evidence: This is supported by quantified behavioral data shown in Figure 5d.

claim: Perampanel-treated larvae remained evenly distributed across the dish during phototaxis assay.
source: Combined results from three independent assays (n = 129–365 larvae per group) are shown in Figure 5d and presented as the percent of larvae found on distal third of the petri dish. For control larvae ~ 70% swam to the distal third within 1 hr, while the perampanel-treated larvae remained evenly distributed across the dish.
evidence: This is supported by quantified behavioral data shown in Figure 5d.

claim: The inability of the perampanel-treated larvae to undergo phototaxis was not the result of an inability to swim.
source: The inability of the perampanel-treated larvae to undergo phototaxis was not the result of an inability to swim, as seen in Video 2 which was taken at 8.9 fps, with and without perampanel.
evidence: This is supported by video data shown in Video 2.

claim: Perampanel treatment had no effect on the light dimming response.
source: Moreover, we observed that perampanel treatment had no effect on the light dimming response (Video 3).
evidence: This is supported by video data shown in Video 3.

claim: The percentage of larvae responding to dimming at all intensities was very similar for control and perampanel-treated groups.
source: To quantitatively compare dimming response, control and perampanel-treated larvae were exposed to a range of dimming intensities from 2 to 60-fold and the percentage of larvae responding was measured and presented as a percentage in Figure 6c (results are from three independent assays, with 46–139 larvae per group). The percentage responding at all intensities was very similar for both groups, and pair-wise comparisons at each fold change failed to show significance.
evidence: This is supported by quantified behavioral data shown in Figure 6c.

claim: No differences were measured in the velocity or duration of swims in pair-wise comparisons of control and perampanel-treated larvae at any fold-dimming.
source: In addition, no differences were measured in the velocity or duration of swims in pair-wise comparisons of control and perampanel-treated larvae at any fold-dimming (data not shown).
evidence: This is supported by the authors' experimental observations.

claim: There is no change in sensitivity to dimming caused by perampanel treatment, while phototaxis was completely disrupted.
source: We conclude that there is no change in sensitivity to dimming caused by perampanel treatment, while phototaxis was completely disrupted.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on behavioral assay data.

claim: The touch response was not inhibited by perampanel.
source: Finally, we also observed that the touch response was not inhibited by perampanel (data not shown), despite the presence of VGLUT-positive epidermal sensory neurons (Horie et al., 2008b).
evidence: This is supported by the authors' experimental observations and citation to Horie et al., 2008b.

claim: The primary RNs for the PNS, the eminens cells and the AMGs, do not express the AMPAR.
source: This would appear to agree with the observation that primary RNs for the PNS, the eminens cells and the AMGs do not express the AMPAR (Hirai et al., 2017; and our observations).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hirai et al., 2017 and the authors' own observations.

claim: The Ciona genome contains one kainate and one NMDA glutamate receptor in addition to the AMPAR.
source: In addition to the AMPAR, the Ciona genome contains several other glutamate receptors including one kainate and one NMDA (Okamura et al., 2005), although their expression has not been characterized.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Okamura et al., 2005.

claim: The expression of kainate and NMDA glutamate receptors has not been characterized in Ciona.
source: In addition to the AMPAR, the Ciona genome contains several other glutamate receptors including one kainate and one NMDA (Okamura et al., 2005), although their expression has not been characterized.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge.

claim: The VACHT/AMPAR-positive RNs are essential for an excitatory PR-I circuit that involves presynaptic glutamatergic PR-Is and postsynaptic cholinergic MGINs.
source: In summary, we are able to separate the phototaxis and dimming behaviors pharmacologically. Moreover, we can identify the VACHT/AMPAR-positive RNs as essential for an excitatory PR-I circuit that involves presynaptic glutamatergic PR-Is and postsynaptic cholinergic MGINs.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on neurotransmitter expression data and pharmacological experiments.

claim: The number and location of the VACHT/AMPAR-positive RNs, the circuit logic, and behavioral observations are all consistent with these being prRNs.
source: The number and location of the VACHT/AMPAR-positive RNs, the circuit logic, and our behavioral observations are all consistent with these being prRNs.
evidence: This is an inference based on multiple lines of evidence.

claim: The dimming response is mediated by the PR-IIs.
source: Of equal significance to our observation that navigation is inhibited by perampanel, is our observation that the dimming response, which is mediated by the PR-IIs (Salas et al., 2018), is not inhibited by perampanel (Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Salas et al., 2018 and behavioral data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Several of the PR-IIs are VGAT-only, as are the majority of the pr-AMG RNs.
source: Although it is formally possible that PR-IIs signal exclusively via glutamate in an excitatory circuit via a non-AMPA glutamate receptor on their RNs, our observations that several of the PR-IIs are VGAT-only, as are the majority of the pr-AMG RNs, suggests an alternative disinhibitory circuitry logic.
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data.

claim: A disinhibitory circuit would consist of the inhibitory PR-IIs synapsing to the pr-AMG RNs to reduce their inhibition on the cholinergic MGINs.
source: This circuit would consist of the inhibitory PR-IIs synapsing to the pr-AMG RNs to reduce their inhibition on the cholinergic MGINs.
evidence: This is a hypothetical model based on neurotransmitter expression patterns.

claim: The disinhibitory model implies an autonomous level of motor activity in larvae that could be inhibited by the GABAergic pr-AMG RNs.
source: Implicit in the disinhibitory model is an autonomous level of motor activity in larvae that could be inhibited by the GABAergic pr-AMG RNs, and that this inhibition is released upon stimulation of the GABAergic PR-IIs.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the disinhibitory model.

claim: Inhibition by GABAergic pr-AMG RNs is released upon stimulation of the GABAergic PR-IIs.
source: Implicit in the disinhibitory model is an autonomous level of motor activity in larvae that could be inhibited by the GABAergic pr-AMG RNs, and that this inhibition is released upon stimulation of the GABAergic PR-IIs.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the disinhibitory model.

claim: Picrotoxin should inhibit signals from the GABAergic photoreceptors and the pr-AMG RNs.
source: In the first approach, we inhibited GABAergic receptors with picrotoxin (Olsen, 2014), which should inhibit signals from the GABAergic photoreceptors and the pr-AMG RNs (and most likely the AntRNs), as well as PNS relay neurons, including the eminens cells and the AMGs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known action of picrotoxin, supported by citation to Olsen, 2014.

claim: The ACINs are glycinergic and should not be inhibited by picrotoxin.
source: The ACINs, which are essential for the central pattern generator (Nishino et al., 2010), are glycinergic and should not be inhibited by picrotoxin.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known action of picrotoxin and citation to Nishino et al., 2010.

claim: In homozygous frm larvae the anterior BV is transfated to epidermis due to a null mutation in a neurula stage-specific connexin gene.
source: In the second approach, we took advantage of a previously described Ciona mutant, frimousse (frm) (Deschet and Smith, 2004; Hackley et al., 2013). In homozygous frm larvae the anterior BV is transfated to epidermis due to a null mutation in a neurula stage-specific connexin gene (Hackley et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Deschet and Smith, 2004 and Hackley et al., 2013.

claim: Frm larvae lack the ocellus pigment cell and photoreceptors, as well as the otolith.
source: Frm larvae thus lack the ocellus pigment cell and photoreceptors, as well as the otolith, although the motor ganglion appears intact (Deschet and Smith, 2004; Hackley et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Deschet and Smith, 2004 and Hackley et al., 2013.

claim: The motor ganglion appears intact in frm larvae.
source: Frm larvae thus lack the ocellus pigment cell and photoreceptors, as well as the otolith, although the motor ganglion appears intact (Deschet and Smith, 2004; Hackley et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Deschet and Smith, 2004 and Hackley et al., 2013.

claim: Ciona larvae display spontaneous swims consisting primarily of short 'tail flicks' when observed under far-red illumination.
source: As reported previously, when observed under far-red illumination (i.e., outside of the larval response range [Nakagawa et al., 1999]) Ciona larvae display spontaneous swims consisting primarily of short 'tail flicks', with very few sustained swims (Salas et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Nakagawa et al., 1999 and Salas et al., 2018.

claim: The frequency of spontaneous swims in the picrotoxin-treated group increased significantly when compared to vehicle-treated (p=2.2×10−16, n = 75 for both).
source: In these conditions, we observed that the frequency of spontaneous swims in the picrotoxin-treated group increased significantly when compared to vehicle-treated (Figure 7a; Video 4; p=2.2×10−16, n = 75 for both).
evidence: This is supported by quantified behavioral data shown in Figure 7a and Video 4.

claim: Overall, the swims for the picrotoxin group were shorter (p=8.8×10−12, n = 184 and 542 for control and picrotoxin respectively).
source: In comparing the duration of the spontaneous swims of the two groups (picrotoxin- and vehicle-treated) we observed an interesting distribution (Figure 7b). Overall, the swims for the picrotoxin group were shorter (p=8.8×10−12, n = 184 and 542 for control and picrotoxin respectively), although the picrotoxin group showed more variation, with a number of long-swimming outliers.
evidence: This is supported by quantified behavioral data shown in Figure 7b.

claim: The picrotoxin group showed more variation in swim duration, with a number of long-swimming outliers.
source: In comparing the duration of the spontaneous swims of the two groups (picrotoxin- and vehicle-treated) we observed an interesting distribution (Figure 7b). Overall, the swims for the picrotoxin group were shorter (p=8.8×10−12, n = 184 and 542 for control and picrotoxin respectively), although the picrotoxin group showed more variation, with a number of long-swimming outliers.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 7b.

claim: Behavioral responses were measured within approximately 20 min of adding picrotoxin (or vehicle only).
source: In the above assays, behavioral responses were measured within ~20 min of adding picrotoxin (or vehicle only).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental protocol.

claim: Longer exposure to picrotoxin (>1 hr) resulted in the nearly complete inhibition of spontaneous and induced swimming behavior.
source: We observed that longer exposure to picrotoxin (>1 hr) resulted in the nearly complete inhibition of spontaneous and induced swimming behavior, presumably due to overactivation at excitatory synapses following removal of inhibitory input.
evidence: This is supported by the authors' experimental observations.

claim: The inhibitory effect of prolonged picrotoxin exposure could be reversed by washing out the picrotoxin.
source: However, this could be reversed by washing out the picrotoxin (data not shown).
evidence: This is supported by the authors' experimental observations.

claim: The picrotoxin-treated larvae did show negative phototaxis when measured at 1 hr, although the response was dampened in comparison to controls (p=8.7×10−4 and p=0.03 for control and picrotoxin respectively, n = 137–487).
source: Nevertheless, the picrotoxin-treated larvae did show negative phototaxis when measured at 1 hr, although the response was dampened in comparison to controls (Figure 7c; p=8.7×10−4 and p=0.03 for control and picrotoxin respectively, n = 137–487; also see Video 5).
evidence: This is supported by quantified behavioral data shown in Figure 7c and Video 5.

claim: The picrotoxin-treated larvae showed a large decrease in evoked sustained swims (defined as lasting longer than 10 s) when assessed for the dimming response.
source: When assessed for the dimming response the picrotoxin-treated larvae showed a large decrease in evoked sustained swims (defined as lasting longer than 10 s) (Figure 7d; Video 6).
evidence: This is supported by quantified behavioral data shown in Figure 7d and Video 6.

claim: A preponderance of very short swims was observed in picrotoxin-treated larvae during dimming response, likely reflecting the elevated rate of spontaneous tail-flick swims.
source: Instead, we observed a preponderance of very short swims that likely reflect the elevated rate of spontaneous tail-flick swims in the larvae.
evidence: This is an inference based on behavioral observations.

claim: There remained a number of sustained swims in the picrotoxin-treated larvae during dimming response.
source: Nevertheless, there remained a number of sustained swims in the picrotoxin-treated larvae.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral observations.

claim: The sustained swims in picrotoxin-treated larvae during dimming response were likely due to a small contribution from the PR-Is to the dimming response.
source: While it is possible that these were due to incomplete inhibition by picrotoxin, we feel it was more likely due to a small contribution from the PR-Is to the dimming response, as we have speculated previously (Salas et al., 2018).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citation to Salas et al., 2018.

claim: Treatment of larvae with picrotoxin and perampanel completely eliminated the evoked sustained swims during dimming response.
source: In support of this, we observed that treatment of larvae with picrotoxin and perampanel completely eliminated the evoked sustained swims.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral assay data.

claim: Swims evoked by the PR-Is have lower tortuosity (are straighter) than those evoked by the PR-IIs.
source: We documented that swims evoked by the PR-Is have lower tortuosity (i.e., are straighter) than those evoked by the PR-IIs (Salas et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Salas et al., 2018.

claim: The tortuosity of the sustained swims from the picrotoxin-treated larvae had lower tortuosity than those of the vehicle-treated controls (n = 19 and 60, respectively; p=0.003).
source: Consistent with this, we found the tortuosity of the sustained swims from the picrotoxin-treated larvae had lower tortuosity than those of the vehicle-treated controls (Figure 7e; n = 19 and 60, respectively; p=0.003).
evidence: This is supported by quantified behavioral data shown in Figure 7e.

claim: Frm larvae showed no response to light.
source: As would be predicted due to their loss of photoreceptors (Hackley et al., 2013), frm larvae showed no response to light (our unpublished observation).
evidence: This is supported by the authors' unpublished observations and citation to Hackley et al., 2013.

claim: The MG is intact in frm larvae as assessed by both gene expression and morphology.
source: Despite the defects in the anterior BV, the MG is intact in frm larvae as assessed by both gene expression and morphology (Deschet and Smith, 2004 and Figure 8a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Deschet and Smith, 2004 and data shown in Figure 8a.

claim: Frm larvae show increased frequency of spontaneous swims compared to wild type larvae (n = 75 for both; p<5×10−16).
source: Moreover, not only can frm larvae swim, they show increased frequency of spontaneous swims compared to wild type larvae (Figure 8b) when assessed using the same parameters as for the picrotoxin-treated larvae (n = 75 for both; p<5×10−16).
evidence: This is supported by quantified behavioral data shown in Figure 8b.

claim: The average swim time was not significantly different between frm and wild type larvae (n = 260 and 608, respectively).
source: Although the frequency of swims was higher in frm larvae, the average swim time was not significantly different between the two (Figure 8c; n = 260 and 608, respectively).
evidence: This is supported by quantified behavioral data shown in Figure 8c.

claim: A handful of very long swims were observed uniquely in the frm group.
source: However as with the picrotoxin-treated larvae, a handful of very long swims were observed uniquely in the frm group (Figure 8c).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 8c.

claim: The swimming of frm larvae is much more stereotyped than wild type larvae.
source: Despite the similarity in the swim times between the frm and wild type larvae, the swim characteristics were very different (Video 7), with the swimming of frm larvae being much more stereotyped.
evidence: This is supported by video data shown in Video 7.

claim: The standard deviations of swim times show much lower swim-to-swim variation in the frm larvae (p<5×10−15).
source: For example, while average swim times of wild type and frm larvae were very similar (Figure 8c), the standard deviations of swim times calculated and plotted for each larva show much lower swim-to-swim variation in the frm larvae (Figure 8d; p<5×10−15).
evidence: This is supported by quantified behavioral data shown in Figure 8d.

claim: The standard deviations of interval times for wild type larvae showed a wide range of values (high variability of interval times), while the standard deviations for frm larvae were much lower (p<0.0005).
source: The stereotypy was even more pronounced when the time interval between swims was analyzed (Figure 8e). For wild type larvae the standard deviations of interval times showed a wide range of values (i.e., high variability of interval times), while the standard deviations for frm larvae were much lower (p<0.0005).
evidence: This is supported by quantified behavioral data shown in Figure 8e.

claim: No increase in stereotypic behavior was observed in comparing picrotoxin- to vehicle-treated larvae.
source: We did not observe an increase in stereotypic behavior in comparing picrotoxin- to vehicle-treated larvae (data not shown).
evidence: This is supported by the authors' experimental observations.

claim: The behavior of frm larvae is characteristic of an oscillator that evokes spontaneous swims with the frequency of approximately 8/min.
source: We did not observe an increase in stereotypic behavior in comparing picrotoxin- to vehicle-treated larvae (data not shown). The behavior of frm larvae is characteristic of an oscillator that evokes spontaneous swims with the frequency of ~8/min.
evidence: This is an inference based on behavioral observations.

claim: Sensory input from the BV appears to suppress oscillatory behavior, leading to less frequent and more varied swims in wt larvae, supporting a disinhibitory circuit.
source: Thus, sensory input from the BV appears to suppress this oscillatory behavior, leading to less frequent and more varied swims in wt larvae, supporting a disinhibitory circuit.
evidence: This is an inference based on behavioral observations of frm mutants.

claim: Some VGAT and VACHT expression was observed in the remnant of the frm BV.
source: Interestingly, we observed some VGAT and VACHT expression in the remnant of the frm BV (Figure 8a).
evidence: This is supported by expression data shown in Figure 8a.

claim: The Ciona PR-I and PR-II visual circuits operate by very different logic.
source: In the current study, we report that the Ciona PR-I and PR-II visual circuits operate by very different logic.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: The PR-I circuit is an excitatory relay from glutamatergic photoreceptors signaling to AMPA receptors on cholinergic prRNs.
source: We find that the PR-I circuit is an excitatory relay from glutamatergic photoreceptors signaling to AMPA receptors on cholinergic prRNs.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on neurotransmitter expression and pharmacological data.

claim: The PR-II circuit initiates with GABAergic photoreceptors synapsing onto GABAergic pr-AMG RNs.
source: On the other hand, the PR-II circuit initiates with GABAergic photoreceptors synapsing onto GABAergic pr-AMG RNs.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on neurotransmitter expression data.

claim: The sequential array of GABAergic neurons in the PR-II pathway supports a model in which this circuit is disinhibitory.
source: Both the sequential array of GABAergic neurons in this pathway and the behavior of larvae treated with GABA inhibitors, or carrying a mutation that misspecifies the anterior BV, support a model in which this circuit is disinhibitory.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on neurotransmitter expression and behavioral data.

claim: A number of other sensory systems, including mammalian vision and olfaction and Drosophila CO2 detection, similarly split components of sensory information into parallel circuits.
source: A number of other sensory systems, including mammalian vision and olfaction and Drosophila CO2 detection (Callaway, 2005; Geramita et al., 2016; Lin et al., 2013) similarly split components of sensory information into parallel circuits.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Callaway, 2005, Geramita et al., 2016, and Lin et al., 2013.

claim: Glutamate is used by the Ciona larvae exclusively in sensory neurons (photoreceptors, antenna cells, and epidermal sensory neurons).
source: The fact that glutamate is used by the Ciona larvae exclusively in sensory neurons (photoreceptors, antenna cells, and epidermal sensory neurons), coupled with the very limited distribution of AMPARs, allowed us to validate essential components of this circuitry with perampanel.
evidence: This is a summary of neurotransmitter expression patterns observed in the study.

claim: The very limited distribution of AMPARs allowed validation of essential components of the PR-I circuitry with perampanel.
source: The fact that glutamate is used by the Ciona larvae exclusively in sensory neurons (photoreceptors, antenna cells, and epidermal sensory neurons), coupled with the very limited distribution of AMPARs, allowed us to validate essential components of this circuitry with perampanel.
evidence: This is an inference about the experimental approach.

claim: The PR-Is also synapse onto the pr-AMG RNs, which are predicted to be primarily GABAergic.
source: The PR-Is also synapse onto the pr-AMG RNs, which are predicted to be primarily GABAergic.
evidence: This is supported by connectome data and neurotransmitter expression predictions.

claim: The response of GABAergic cells to the PR-Is may differ from cholinergic cells.
source: Our observation that AMPAR expression is exclusive to the cholinergic RNs suggests that the response of GABAergic cells to the PR-Is may differ from cholinergic cells, and perhaps plays a role in visual information processing.
evidence: This is speculation based on neurotransmitter expression patterns.

claim: The interconnections between the pr-AMG RNs and the AMPAR-expressing prRNs are suggestive of an incoherent feedforward loop.
source: In fact, the interconnections between the pr-AMG RNs and the AMPAR-expressing prRNs (black arrow Figure 9; see also Figure 1—figure supplement 1), are suggestive of an incoherent feedforward loop (Alon, 2007).
evidence: This is an inference based on circuit connectivity, supported by citation to Alon, 2007.

claim: Ciona larvae are able to phototax in a wide range of illumination conditions.
source: We have already documented that Ciona larvae are able to phototax in a wide range of illumination conditions (Salas et al., 2018), and moreover, we have found that Ciona larvae show robust fold-change detection (Adler and Alon, 2018) behavior (manuscript in preparation).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Salas et al., 2018.

claim: Ciona larvae show robust fold-change detection behavior.
source: We have already documented that Ciona larvae are able to phototax in a wide range of illumination conditions (Salas et al., 2018), and moreover, we have found that Ciona larvae show robust fold-change detection (Adler and Alon, 2018) behavior (manuscript in preparation).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Adler and Alon, 2018 and reference to a manuscript in preparation.

claim: The RN cluster plays a role in visual processing, rather than simply passing information to the MG.
source: Together these observations suggest that the RN cluster plays a role in visual processing, rather than simply passing information to the MG.
evidence: This is an inference based on circuit connectivity and behavioral observations.

claim: The Ciona PR-II mediated dimming/escape behavior includes a novelty – inhibitory photoreceptors.
source: Our model for the PR-II mediated dimming/escape behavior is more surprising, and includes a novelty – inhibitory photoreceptors.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the novelty of the findings.

claim: Similar coexpression of VGAT and VGLUT is widely observed in mammalian brains and invertebrates.
source: The significance of VGAT/VGLUT coexpression in the Ciona visuomotor pathway is not yet clear, although similar coexpression is widely observed in mammalian brains (Fattorini et al., 2015; Zander et al., 2010) and invertebrates (Fabian-Fine et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fattorini et al., 2015, Zander et al., 2010, and Fabian-Fine et al., 2015.

claim: It is speculated that co-release of GABA and GLUT may serve to tune excitatory/inhibitory balance.
source: It is speculated that co-release of GABA and GLUT may serve to tune excitatory/inhibitory balance.
evidence: This is speculation about the function of neurotransmitter coexpression.

claim: The Ciona genome encodes seven ionotropic/Cl- GABA receptor subunit genes (GABAA).
source: The Ciona genome encodes seven ionotropic/Cl- GABA receptor subunit genes (GABAA) (Okamura et al., 2005), but does not have an ortholog of the cationic EXP-1 GABA receptor (Beg and Jorgensen, 2003), confirmation that the GABAergic synaptic events are most likely inhibitory.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Okamura et al., 2005 and Beg and Jorgensen, 2003.

claim: The Ciona genome does not have an ortholog of the cationic EXP-1 GABA receptor.
source: The Ciona genome encodes seven ionotropic/Cl- GABA receptor subunit genes (GABAA) (Okamura et al., 2005), but does not have an ortholog of the cationic EXP-1 GABA receptor (Beg and Jorgensen, 2003), confirmation that the GABAergic synaptic events are most likely inhibitory.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Beg and Jorgensen, 2003.

claim: GABAergic synaptic events in Ciona are most likely inhibitory.
source: The Ciona genome encodes seven ionotropic/Cl- GABA receptor subunit genes (GABAA) (Okamura et al., 2005), but does not have an ortholog of the cationic EXP-1 GABA receptor (Beg and Jorgensen, 2003), confirmation that the GABAergic synaptic events are most likely inhibitory.
evidence: This is an inference based on the types of GABA receptors present in the genome.

claim: Electrophysiological studies on larvae of the ascidian Amaroucium constellatum reported that their photoreceptors, like those of vertebrates, were hyperpolarizing.
source: In addition, electrophysiological studies done nearly fifty years ago on larvae of the ascidian Amaroucium constellatum reported that their photoreceptors, like those of vertebrates, were hyperpolarizing (Gorman et al., 1971).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gorman et al., 1971.

claim: Dimming is likely to result in a release of GABA from the PR-IIs.
source: In other words, dimming is likely to result in a release of GABA from the PR-IIs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the hyperpolarizing nature of photoreceptors and GABAergic identity of PR-IIs.

claim: The vertebrate-like ciliary structure shared by all Ciona photoreceptors and the structure of Ciona opsins appear to rule out the possibility of depolarizing phototransduction.
