source: Although the heterogeneity of ascidian photoreceptors (e.g., PR-I and –II) was not known at the time, both the vertebrate-like ciliary structure shared by all Ciona photoreceptors and the structure of Ciona opsins appear to rule out the possibility of depolarizing phototransduction (Kusakabe and Tsuda, 2007; Kusakabe et al., 2001).
evidence: This is an inference based on photoreceptor structure, supported by citations to Kusakabe and Tsuda, 2007 and Kusakabe et al., 2001.

claim: Removal of BV sensory input with the frm mutant leads to more frequent spontaneous swims, suggesting that a disinhibitory pathway could lead to stimulation of swimming.
source: Also in agreement with an inhibitory output from the PR-IIs is our prediction that the majority of the pr-AMG RNs, the exclusive RNs of the PR-IIs, are themselves GABAergic, which would make a disinhibitory circuit most plausible (Figure 9). We also show that removal of BV sensory input with the frm mutant, or inhibition of GABA receptors with picrotoxin, leads to more frequent spontaneous swims, suggesting that a disinhibitory pathway could lead to stimulation of swimming.
evidence: This is an inference based on behavioral data from frm mutants.

claim: Inhibition of GABA receptors with picrotoxin leads to more frequent spontaneous swims, suggesting that a disinhibitory pathway could lead to stimulation of swimming.
source: We also show that removal of BV sensory input with the frm mutant, or inhibition of GABA receptors with picrotoxin, leads to more frequent spontaneous swims, suggesting that a disinhibitory pathway could lead to stimulation of swimming.
evidence: This is an inference based on behavioral data from picrotoxin treatment.

claim: The AMGs are one of the primary relay centers for the PNS and project to the MGINs and MNs.
source: Finally, we observed that the AMGs, with the exception of one cell, are GABAergic. The AMGs are one of the primary relay centers for the PNS (Ryan et al., 2018) and project to the MGINs and MNs.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ryan et al., 2018.

claim: The AMGs project ascending axons to the pr-AMG RNs.
source: However, the AMGs also project ascending axons to the pr-AMG RNs.
evidence: This is supported by connectome data.

claim: The convergence of PR-II and AMG inputs at the pr-AMG RNs serves to initiate an integrated escape response.
source: It is thought that the convergence of PR-II and AMG inputs at the pr-AMG RNs serves to initiate an integrated escape response (Ryan et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ryan et al., 2018.

claim: The finding that PR-IIs and AMGs are likely to have the same input (inhibition) on the pr-AMG RNs further bolsters the integrated response model.
source: Our finding that these two classes of neurons (PR-IIs and AMGs) are likely to have the same input (inhibition) on the pr-AMG RNs further bolsters the integrated response model.
evidence: This is an inference based on neurotransmitter expression patterns.

claim: The PR-II glutamate release at pr-AMG RNs acts through other receptors, such as the NMDA receptor, and may be more involved in modulating or processing the visual response.
source: Finally, the PR-II mediated dimming response was not inhibited by the AMPAR antagonist perampanel, suggesting the PR-II glutamate release at pr-AMG RNs acts through other receptors, such as the NMDA receptor, and may be more involved in modulating or processing the visual response, and that GABA release may be more important.
evidence: This is speculation based on pharmacological experiments.

claim: GABA release from PR-IIs may be more important than glutamate release for the dimming response.
source: Finally, the PR-II mediated dimming response was not inhibited by the AMPAR antagonist perampanel, suggesting the PR-II glutamate release at pr-AMG RNs acts through other receptors, such as the NMDA receptor, and may be more involved in modulating or processing the visual response, and that GABA release may be more important.
evidence: This is speculation based on pharmacological experiments.

claim: The relationship between the ascidian ocellus and the visual organs of cephalochordates and vertebrates remains unclear.
source: The evolutionary relationship between the ascidian ocellus and the visual organs of cephalochordates (e.g., amphioxus) and vertebrates remains unclear (Kusakabe and Tsuda, 2007; Lamb et al., 2007; Lamb, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kusakabe and Tsuda, 2007, Lamb et al., 2007, and Lamb, 2013.

claim: The Ciona PR-I and PR-II complexes may have independent origins and thus have different evolutionary relationships to the photoreceptor organs of other chordates.
source: The observations that the Ciona PR-I and PR-II complexes are distinct morphologically, mediate different behaviors, project via distinct visuomotor circuits, and express different NTs, raises the possibility that these two complexes may have independent origins, and thus have different evolutionary relationships to the photoreceptor organs of other chordates.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed differences between PR-I and PR-II.

claim: The ascidian PR-I complex is likely to be homologous to the vertebrate lateral eyes and the amphioxus frontal eye.
source: We speculate that the ascidian PR-I complex is likely to be homologous to the vertebrate lateral eyes and the amphioxus frontal eye, which like the PR-I complex is pigmented and appears to play a role in detecting the direction of light, although not necessarily in taxis (Stokes and Holland, 1995).
evidence: This is speculation based on functional and morphological similarities, supported by citation to Stokes and Holland, 1995.

claim: The pineal eyes of amphibian tadpoles and fish larvae mediate a shadow/dimming response, suggesting homology with the ascidian PR-II photoreceptor complex.
source: On the other hand, the pineal eyes of amphibian tadpoles and fish larvae mediate a shadow/dimming response, suggesting homology with the ascidian PR-II photoreceptor complex (Jamieson and Roberts, 2000; Yoshizawa and Jeffery, 2008).
evidence: This is speculation based on functional similarities, supported by citations to Jamieson and Roberts, 2000 and Yoshizawa and Jeffery, 2008.

claim: The inhibitory nature of the Ciona PR-IIs makes assigning homologies more difficult.
source: Nevertheless, the inhibitory nature of the Ciona PR-IIs makes assigning homologies more difficult.
evidence: This is a statement about the challenges in evolutionary interpretation.

claim: Use of GABA by PR-II photoreceptors may be a derived feature of ascidians, as inhibitory photoreceptors have yet to be described elsewhere.
source: It is possible that use of GABA by these photoreceptors is a derived feature of ascidians, as inhibitory photoreceptors have yet to be described elsewhere.
evidence: This is speculation about the evolutionary origin of GABAergic photoreceptors.

claim: In the vertebrate retina GABAergic/glycinergic horizontal and amacrine cells are prevalent.
source: Alternatively, in the vertebrate retina GABAergic/glycinergic horizontal and amacrine cells are prevalent, and, moreover, it has been proposed that these cells, as well as ganglion cells, are derived from an ancient photoreceptor (Lamb, 2013; Arendt, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lamb, 2013 and Arendt, 2003.

claim: It has been proposed that horizontal cells, amacrine cells, and ganglion cells in the vertebrate retina are derived from an ancient photoreceptor.
source: Alternatively, in the vertebrate retina GABAergic/glycinergic horizontal and amacrine cells are prevalent, and, moreover, it has been proposed that these cells, as well as ganglion cells, are derived from an ancient photoreceptor (Lamb, 2013; Arendt, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lamb, 2013 and Arendt, 2003.

claim: The observations about GABAergic cells in vertebrate retina may simply support the plasticity of NT use in visual systems.
source: While this may imply an alternative evolutionary origin for the Ciona PR-IIs, these observations may simply support the plasticity of NT use in visual systems.
evidence: This is speculation about the evolutionary interpretation of neurotransmitter use.
